ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.24: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Power-assist Mechanism. Manual wheelchair use may cause shoulder injuries. Power-assist wheels amplify the user's pushing force. COURSE LOGIC - Distinguish reduced propulsion endurance from inability to steer safely. If a user retains usable pushing but needs a wheelchair throughout a long day, limited arm strength or stamina can favor power-assist over an unassisted manual chair. Smart sensing is supported by evidence of difficulty with navigation, obstacle avoidance or ordinary driving, not by all-day use or a spinal-cord-injury label alone. A completely absent reliable push instead calls for powered propulsion; do not infer residual pushing solely from the diagnosis. This distinction is also supported by the instructor's graded mobility example, while the slide itself establishes the push-amplification mechanism.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.32: COURSE LOGIC - The slide defines a smart wheelchair as either a standard power wheelchair augmented with a computer and sensors or a mobile-robot base with a seat. It is useful when low vision/restricted visual field, motor impairments such as excessive tone or tremor, or cognitive impairments make safe ordinary wheelchair navigation difficult. Therefore selection follows the functional control problem: inability to self-propel points toward powered mobility, while difficulty safely navigating or controlling an ordinary power chair supports adding smart sensing/computer assistance; the diagnosis alone is not sufficient.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.34:
VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchairs have two functions. Collision avoidance: sensors detect an obstacle in the wheelchair path and slow or stop the chair or warn the user if no avoidance maneuver is performed. Navigation along a path or through obstacles: sensors guide the chair along a programmed or environmental pathway, or through a feature such as a doorway.

COURSE LOGIC - Smart-wheelchair sensors support two core functions: collision/obstacle avoidance and navigation. Candidate sensors are judged by whether they measure distance, motion, contact or orientation for those functions; infrared, ultrasonic and inertial sensors are explicitly used examples. Do not treat every sensor type as an answer merely because it is a possible engineering component.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.37:
VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchair Sensors, Table 5.1. No sensor or sensor combination meets all requirements for accuracy, low cost, small/light size, environmental robustness and low power. Ultrasonic/sonar uses sound to measure obstacle distance: small, low-power and low-cost, but sensitive to absorbing, thin or concave surfaces, crosstalk, drop-off hazards unless aimed down and limited coverage. Infrared (IR) uses light for distance sensing or light/dark transitions: small, low-power and low-cost, but affected by natural light, floor-surface errors and limited coverage. Laser range finder performs a 180-degree environmental-distance scan: high precision and long range, but costly, power-consuming, subject to eye-safety constraints and measures only at installation height. Stereovision camera produces colour/black-and-white images plus depth: low power and medium cost, supports scene recognition and head/eye tracking, but struggles with textureless scenes, poor light, reflective or transparent surfaces.

COURSE LOGIC - The explicit smart-wheelchair sensor list spans pages 37-38: ultrasonic/sonar, infrared, laser range finder, stereovision camera, structured light, BUMP tactile sensor, wheelchair encoders, IMU and GPS. For a question asking which sensors are named on this list, use this closed device-context list; do not import a sensor from another lecture because it is technically plausible. A BUMP/tactile sensor reports obstacle contact, whereas a generic force sensor is not a named smart-wheelchair sensor category on these slides. Hall-effect sensors are likewise not named on this list.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.38: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchair Sensors continued. Structured light (Microsoft Kinect) projects infrared for image and depth: low-power/low-cost with scene/head/eye understanding, but outdoor IR interference, glass misses and high computation. BUMP tactile sensor detects contact when an object exerts force on the bumper: low-cost/low-power, but requires contact and a wide bumper can be bulky. Wheelchair encoders measure wheel rotation/count and speed to estimate distance/speed: retrofit can be costly and wheel slip causes error. IMUs combine accelerometers, gyroscopes and optional magnetometers to estimate velocity, orientation and position: low-cost/low-power but drift; high-accuracy units cost more. GPS supplies location and time, works with unobstructed satellites at low cost but poorly indoors.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.39: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchair Input Methods. Brain-computer interface using EEG or ECoG. Eye gaze uses cameras to determine steering. Voice recognition interprets steering commands.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.40: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchair Feedback Modalities. Speakers provide audio feedback. Small LEDs provide visual feedback such as flashing red when close to an object. Haptic feedback uses small vibrations to warn about obstacles. Touch screen displays gather driver input such as destination and display scheduled activities, way-finding assistance and virtual environments.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.41: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchair Feedback Modalities continued. Auditory feedback uses warning sirens, distance tones or spoken words. Visual feedback uses lights or a dashboard. Haptic feedback uses pressure applied to a joystick.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.42: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smart Wheelchair Control. The slide describes autonomous and shared or semiautonomous control. COURSE LOGIC - The user and onboard computer both contribute under shared control; under autonomous control, the computer assumes full control. Select among manual, power-assist, ordinary power and smart wheelchairs by the required function. Manual propulsion requires strength, coordination and endurance. Power-assist amplifies residual pushing when long-duration effort or fatigue is the bottleneck. Ordinary power supplies propulsion when pushing is unavailable but reliable driving commands remain. Smart features add navigation and collision avoidance when ordinary driving or navigation is difficult. Limited arm function or an SCI label alone does not establish unsafe navigation, and all-day mobility need alone does not imply smart control. Retain the user's functional abilities and stated task as the deciding evidence; do not assign a device from a diagnosis or from an unsupported assumption about joystick or pushing ability. For questions about smart-chair control itself, distinguish shared input from autonomous control using the described functions.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.50: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smile Smart System Key System Elements. Controls provide input options. Bumper protects chair and driver. Sensors detect objects to avoid collisions. Tape provides guidance to steer the powerchair.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.53: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Smile Smart System Personal Drive Prescription. Elements include Scanner, Joystick, Switches, Softytops, 100mm Switch adapter, Flexi-rod, Switch mount and Drive assist.
ME5412 2. Mobility aids.pdf.54: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Robotic technology versus assistive device exam interpretation. For the question Which robotic technologies can contribute to assistive technologies? select Navigation. Navigation is a robotic enabling capability that can be added to an assistive device such as a power wheelchair, together with obstacle avoidance and shared control, to make a smart wheelchair. Exoskeleton is a robotic assistive device/product category, not the underlying robotic capability requested by this wording. Manufacturing is an industrial application area; Automation is too broad and is not the specific course capability named here. Therefore the intended answer is Navigation.

ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.3: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Regions of the human body. Anterior/frontal regions include the cranium or skull, face, eye, cheek, ear, nose, neck, chest/thorax, breast, abdomen, umbilicus, hip, pelvis, groin, pubis, thigh/femur, knee/patella, leg/crus, ankle/tarsus, foot/sole and toes. Posterior regions include head, neck, back/dorsum, shoulder, arm/brachium, elbow/olecranon, forearm/antebrachium, hand/manus, buttock/gluteus, thigh/femur, knee, calf/sura, heel/calcaneus and sole/planta.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.4: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Directional Terms. Anterior or ventral means toward the front; posterior or dorsal means toward the back; superior or cranial means above; inferior or caudal means below; lateral means toward the side; medial means toward the body's middle; proximal means nearer the point of attachment or trunk; distal means farther from the point of attachment or trunk; superficial means closer to the body surface; deep means farther from the surface.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.5: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Body Planes. The sagittal plane divides the body vertically into right and left; the midsagittal or median plane divides it into equal right and left halves, while a parasagittal plane divides unequal sides. The frontal or coronal plane divides the body into anterior/front and posterior/rear portions. The transverse plane divides the body horizontally into upper and lower portions and produces cross sections.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.6: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Axial skeleton. The axial skeleton forms the vertical central axis and includes the bones of the head, neck, chest and back. It protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs and provides muscle attachment. The adult axial skeleton has 80 bones, including the skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage; the skull has 22 bones, the vertebral column has 24 vertebrae plus sacrum and coccyx, and the thoracic cage has 12 pairs of ribs and the sternum.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.8: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Types of Joints. Pivot joints allow rotation around an axis, such as between C1 and C2. The elbow is a hinge joint. The thumb carpometacarpal articulation is a saddle joint. Plane joints, such as between tarsal bones, allow limited gliding. The radiocarpal wrist joint is a condyloid joint. The hip and shoulder are ball-and-socket joints.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.9: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Types of Movements. Movements shown include pronation and supination, dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, inversion and eversion, protraction and retraction, elevation and depression, opposition, flexion and extension, abduction and adduction, circumduction, and medial and lateral rotation.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.10: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - The vertebral column. Also called the spinal column or spine, it consists of vertebrae separated and united by intervertebral discs. It supports the head, neck and body, allows movement, and protects the spinal cord as it passes through openings in the vertebrae. It includes cervical, thoracic and lumbar regions, plus the sacrum and coccyx.
ME5412 4. Anatomy SCI assessment.pdf.11: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Regions of the vertebral column. The vertebral column begins as 33 vertebrae and becomes 24 vertebrae plus the sacrum and coccyx. It has five regions: 7 cervical vertebrae C1-C7, 12 thoracic vertebrae T1-T12, 5 lumbar vertebrae L1-L5, 5 fused sacral vertebrae forming the sacrum, and 4 small fused coccygeal vertebrae forming the coccyx.

2.1 ME5412 Stroke and Stroke Rehabilitat.8: COURSE LOGIC - Stroke type. Ischemic stroke is caused by reduced blood supply because a cerebral blood vessel is blocked. Hemorrhagic stroke is caused by bleeding after a blood vessel ruptures. Do not interchange blockage/ischemia with rupture/hemorrhage; both can injure brain tissue, but the mechanism distinguishes the terms.

2.1 ME5412 Stroke and Stroke Rehabilitat.13: COURSE LOGIC - Hemiparesis means muscular weakness or partial paralysis restricted to one side of the body, usually affecting the upper and lower limb on that side. It is different from paraplegia (both lower limbs) and quadriplegia/tetraplegia (all four limbs). For a typical post-stroke gait, reduced loading on the affected side may produce weight shift to the unaffected side and circumduction of the affected leg to clear the foot.

2.1 ME5412 Stroke and Stroke Rehabilitat.17: COURSE LOGIC - Neuroplasticity is the capacity of neural pathways and synapses to change with experience, injury and training. In stroke rehabilitation, properly stimulated unused or undamaged motor areas can be recruited or reorganized to take over functions of damaged areas. It does not mean that new brain cells necessarily grow, that the damaged area simply returns to normal, or that therapy should reduce plasticity.

2.1 ME5412 Stroke and Stroke Rehabilitat.19: COURSE LOGIC - Rehabilitation goals after stroke include reducing spasticity, inhibiting atypical muscle synergies, preventing contractures and improving functional outcomes through meaningful, repeated training. Learned non-use is addressed by encouraging safe use of the affected limb. Neuroplasticity is facilitated, not reduced; the healthy limb is not expected to do every daily task instead of the affected limb.

ME5412 1. Principles Assistive Technolog.10:
COURSE LOGIC - ICF case reasoning (based on WHO international classifications slides on pages 10, 13 and 14). Keep capacity and performance separate. Activity limitation concerns the underlying capacity for a task, such as walking or climbing stairs. Performance concerns what the person actually accomplishes in a particular environment with an aid. A wheelchair, elevator or accessible route may let a person with a mobility impairment reach a destination and participate, while the underlying limitation in walking or stair climbing remains. An environmental facilitator improves performance and can remove participation restriction; it does not prove that the impairment or activity limitation disappeared. Conversely, an inaccessible building or transport route can be an environmental barrier. Do not infer participation restriction solely from an impairment or activity limitation, and do not invent an unstated barrier.

EXAM CLASSIFICATION METHOD - Preserve every literal fact and negation. (1) Body structure/function problem, such as paralysis or weakness -> Impairment. (2) Concrete task/capacity the person cannot perform, such as walking or climbing stairs -> Activity Limitation, even if an assistive device or accessible route helps performance. (3) Social-life role/outcome, such as inability to leave home, attend work/school or join community activities -> Participation Restriction. Then use environmental factors to decide whether participation is restricted: elevators, ramps, accessible transport, caregivers, policies, assistive devices and wheelchair access may facilitate participation; inaccessible buildings or transport may be barriers. This is a general ICF reasoning framework, not a rule tied to one question.

VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - WHO international classifications. ICIDH (1980): Impairment -> Disability -> Handicap. ICIDH2 (1997): Impairment (functional or structural) -> Limitation of Activity -> Restriction of Participation; terms were reversed to positive terms and the model highlighted social barriers. ICF (2001): Health, body functions/structures, activities and participation interact bidirectionally with Environmental Factors and Personal Factors. Environmental factors can be barriers or facilitators, and assistive technology often changes activity and participation without removing impairment.

DETAILED COURSE LOGIC - ICIDH 1980 is a linear deficit model: impairment is a body structure/function problem; disability is inability/difficulty performing an activity; handicap is restriction of a social role. ICIDH2 uses more neutral functional terms. ICF is a biopsychosocial interaction model: health condition, impairment, activity and participation are not a fixed one-way chain; contextual environmental and personal factors affect their interaction. Personal factors include age, motivation, experience, education, preference and lifestyle.
ME5412 1. Principles Assistive Technolog.12: VISUAL SUPPLEMENT - Case figures ask whether pictured people have impairment, disability, handicap or participation limitations; classification depends on the activity and context.
ME5412 1. Principles Assistive Technolog.13: COURSE LOGIC - ICIDH2 (1997) terminology from the slide. Impairment is considered in functional and structural aspects; activity limitation describes limitation in performing activities, while participation restriction describes restriction in social participation. These are different levels. An environmental barrier can affect participation even when the underlying impairment is unchanged. Evaluate the activity described and the social participation outcome separately rather than collapsing them into one label.
ME5412 1. Principles Assistive Technolog.14: COURSE LOGIC - ICF (2001) bio-psycho-social model from the slide. Disability reflects negative aspects of interaction between a health condition and contextual environmental/personal factors; functioning reflects positive or neutral aspects of that interaction. A facilitator or assistive technology can improve what a person actually does in an environment and their participation without curing the underlying impairment or automatically restoring the person's capacity for every activity. Classify impairment, activity and participation separately, then account for environmental and personal factors.

An expanded keyboard offers larger, more separated direct targets when those targets can be reached and selected accurately enough; a contracted keyboard reduces the movement range needed to reach keys. COURSE LOGIC - Enlargement retains direct selection: the user still reaches and presses the intended key, but its larger target may accommodate imprecise movement. In the graded cerebral-palsy fine-control scenario, larger targets fit the described remaining direct-targeting ability. COURSE LOGIC - An indirect interface inserts a selection process between the user and the target. Scanning highlights choices sequentially; the user activates a switch when the desired choice is highlighted. It is useful when direct pointing or many simultaneous inputs are not reliable, including residual head movement control of a multi-DOF robot. ME5412 3. Assistive Technology Interface.26: COURSE LOGIC - Match the selection method to reliable actions, not merely usable hands or diagnosis. Enlargement preserves direct key selection while making each target easier to hit; scanning substitutes indirect sequential choice for many direct key presses. The graded cerebral-palsy fine-control scenario fits enlarged targets because direct targeting remains viable with larger keys. The graded incomplete-SCI typing scenario fits two-switch step scanning because direct typing is too inaccurate while two simple, distinct actions remain reliable: one switch advances and the other selects (page 17). These are functional distinctions for the described cases, not universal CP or SCI mappings. If enlarged targets cannot be selected reliably, assess scanning; if direct selection is reliable, scanning's extra steps may be unnecessary.
